items.headline: EU AI Act Article 50 reaches its date and starts applying, and the Commission names the AI Office, national market surveillance authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor as the enforcers
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday this was a scheduled catalyst one day out — the transparency obligations "begin to apply tomorrow, Sunday, August 2." Today is that day, and the state-change is that the rule moved from dated to live and acquired named enforcers. The four situations Article 50 covers are the same four yesterday's report listed: a system that interacts directly with a person has to say it is an AI, synthetic image, audio, video and text has to carry machine-readable marks, deployers of emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems have to tell the people exposed to them, and deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest have to be labelled. What is new is everything around that text. The Commission marked the date by confirming enforcement is running and by saying who runs it: national market surveillance authorities, the AI Office, and — a body absent from yesterday's account entirely — the European Data Protection Supervisor. The penalty line gains a second tier. Yesterday carried the €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover ceiling, whichever is higher; today adds €750,000 for EU institutions, bodies and agencies, so the Union's own institutions sit inside the regime they wrote, with proportionality for small and medium enterprises written into the framework. And the compliance scaffolding turns out to predate the date rather than arrive with it: the Commission adopted its Article 50 guidelines on Monday, July 20, thirteen days before the obligation they interpret started applying, and the voluntary Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content — the route a provider can take to demonstrate compliance, carrying a free EU icon set for labelling — has passed 180 signatories with a first list published. Neither the guidelines nor the Code appears anywhere in yesterday's report, so a reader who had only that report knew what the rule says and not that there was already a published way to satisfy it. Two things yesterday's report carried have dropped out of today's account. Yesterday described a narrow grace period under Article 50(2), giving systems already placed on the market until December 2 this year to implement machine-readable marking; and yesterday framed today as the surviving half of a divided deadline, with the Digital Omnibus having pushed stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems to December 2, 2027 and high-risk AI embedded in regulated products to August 2, 2028. Neither survives into today's text, and both rest entirely on yesterday's sourcing — nothing in today's bullet restates either one. The consequence for a reader is that today's report reads as though the whole of the August 2 date arrived with no transitional period attached to any part of it. That is a gap between the two days rather than a contradiction: today's bullet asserts nothing incompatible with either, it simply stops carrying them, and a reader who has only today's report would not know a marking extension had ever been reported. One anchor is new and puts the rest in scale: the AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024, which makes today two years and a day.

items.headline: California's AI Transparency Act becomes operative on the same day as Article 50, because a second bill moved the date there on purpose
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday's report carried exactly one regulatory item and it was European; nothing in it pointed at a US rule, at California, or at a second regime landing on the same date. Today the EU deadline turns out to have a twin, and the twinning was engineered rather than coincidental: SB 942 as passed set the chapter to become operative on January 1, 2026, and AB 853 rewrote that clause to read August 2, 2026 — seven months and a day later, and exactly the day Article 50 starts applying in Brussels. The compliance surface facing a generative-AI provider did not simply go live between yesterday and today; it went live twice. The two rules are not copies of each other, and the differences are the reading. California's binds only above a threshold — a generative system with more than one million monthly visitors or users, publicly accessible in California — where Article 50 sets no size floor at all. California covers images, video and audio; the EU list includes text, which California's latent-disclosure duty does not. California specifies its disclosure down to the fields: provider name, system name and version, the time and date the content was created or altered, and a unique identifier, plus a visible label the user may optionally switch on. And it carries an obligation with no counterpart in either day's account of the EU rule — the provider must publish a free detection tool that supports an application programming interface a user can invoke without visiting the provider's own website, which takes a URL, returns whatever provenance data it finds, and does not retain what was submitted longer than it needs to. Marking is what Brussels asks for; marking plus a public detector anyone can call is what Sacramento asks for. The licensing clause is the sharpest edge: a provider that licenses its system out has to require the same latent-disclosure capability by contract and revoke the licence within 96 hours — four days — of discovering the licensee stripped it. The enforcement shapes diverge as well. The EU ceiling scales with the company and is pursued by state bodies; California's is $5,000 per violation with each day of non-compliance counted separately, no cap stated, brought by the Attorney General or a city attorney or a county counsel, with fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff — so exposure grows with how long the failure runs and how many items it touches rather than with how large the defendant is. Two further tranches are already dated behind it: generative-AI hosting platforms and large online platforms on January 1, 2027, and capture device manufacturers on January 1, 2028. The report's centre of gravity moved with it. Yesterday five of eight items were laboratory or infrastructure work — proofs, a checker, a checkpoint, a harness, an intrusion postmortem — and regulation appeared once, sixth of eight. Today regulation leads twice. The agent-security storyline that ran through yesterday's Tailscale account of the Hugging Face intrusion, and the Y Combinator harness carried beside it, both stop here with no successor.

items.headline: Unsloth publishes 2026.8.1 to PyPI with DeepSeek-V4 0731 support and repins both installers the same day, ending the four-day stall at 2026.7.6
items.diff_narrative: This is the one subject carried directly from yesterday, and the number that would not move is the number that moved. Yesterday's item closed on the published state: twenty-two pull requests merged, none of it shipped, the newest PyPI wheel still 2026.7.6 from July 29 and no 2026.7.7 in existence in either place. Today 2026.8.1 is on PyPI, the first new version since 2026.7.6 — four days, Wednesday to Sunday — and the missing 2026.7.7 is resolved by never being used at all: the project skipped the number and moved the month field instead. The licence and interpreter range are exactly where they were, Apache-2.0 and Python 3.9 up to but not including 3.15, so nothing about who can install it changed; what changed is that there is something new to install. The changelog gives the release three lines and the first closes a loop from yesterday's own report: support for DeepSeek-V4 0731 — written that way in the changelog, where yesterday's report had it as the V4-Flash 0731 build DeepSeek moved out of preview on Friday, the same date stamp either way. Yesterday that checkpoint swap was described as silent, a new model behind an unchanged API name; a trainer picking it up two days later is the first downstream consequence of that swap to appear in this corpus. The other two changelog lines are a batch of Windows fixes and general bug fixes, and Windows is the through-line across both days: yesterday one of the three CI failures blocking every open pull request was a clean-machine Windows container row asserting the released wheel would fail to install, and today's escaping work is in part a Windows-path bug — an unescaped backslash was silently decoded, so `\boxed{}` came out as a backspace followed by `oxed{}` and a path like `C:\Users\me` broke outright, alongside an apostrophe in something like "user's question" closing a Jinja string literal early and raising a template syntax error. Those two merges are the substantive work of the day, and the second carries the number worth keeping: promoting the escape helper to module level, extending it to double quotes and applying it to the system message substituted into the predefined chat templates took successful renderings from 76 of 180 to 180 of 180 across fifteen predefined templates and twelve test messages, which means 104 of the 180 combinations had been failing — well over half, on a path every caller crosses. Yesterday's merges were about getting the test suite to agree; today's are about what the library does when someone types an apostrophe. And one merge finishes the release rather than describing it: later the same day the pin in both `install.sh` and `install.ps1` went to `unsloth>=2026.8.1` and `unsloth-zoo>=2026.8.1` across all five install paths, so a fresh install resolves to the new packages the day they exist rather than trailing them by a cycle. One surface yesterday tracked is not re-checked today: yesterday's report also gave the newest GitHub release as v0.1.51-beta from July 29, and today's item speaks only to PyPI, so the release tag is unstated in either direction.

items.headline: Karpathy runs a two-hour, million-token Tolkien render on Claude Opus 5 and says the field is starting to leave the pelican-on-a-bicycle prompt behind
items.diff_narrative: Nothing in yesterday's report anticipated this, and the contrast with yesterday's lead is the reason to carry it. Yesterday's headline capability claim arrived with ten formal results, a Lean 4 formalisation for every one of them and a per-result spend put at under $2,000; today's most-discussed item is a test with no score, no certificate and no benchmark table in it anywhere. Andrej Karpathy handed Claude Opus 5 the opening paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, a budget of one million tokens costing roughly $10, and a request for a three.js rendering. The model worked for about two hours and returned roughly 5,500 lines of code that procedurally rendered the passage, placing and animating polygon assets in three-dimensional coordinates. Karpathy called the result janky but fun and said the field is starting to leave the territory where you would test a model by asking it for an SVG of a pelican on a bicycle. The denominator problem runs the opposite way from yesterday's. Yesterday's ten results could each be re-executed against an independent checker but withheld the count of attempts that produced nothing; today's run cannot be scored at all and does not pretend otherwise — the measurement is whether an unattended two-hour stretch of work holds together, which is a judgement by construction rather than a figure. Both days state a price, which makes them comparable: under $2,000 a result yesterday against about $10 today, up to two hundred times apart at the ceiling of OpenAI's own number, for output nobody has to verify. One rate falls out of today's own figures if that budget was actually consumed — a million tokens across about two hours is roughly 139 tokens per second sustained for two unattended hours, which is the kind of number that stopped being expensive only recently, and is why a test shaped like this can now be run for fun rather than budgeted for.

items.headline: A Kimi K3 benchmark puts eight MI355X ahead of eight B300 on tokens per dollar and behind on every raw-speed number, with speculative decoding described on only one side of the comparison
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday's report contained no hardware measurement of any kind. The only AMD-against-NVIDIA content anywhere in it was a session list — Hot Chips carrying NVIDIA's Rubin, AMD's Instinct MI400 Series and Intel's Crescent Island in a conference programme three weeks out, inside the events bullet. Today that comparison arrives as numbers on parts that already ship, and it splits. Kimi K3, at 2.8 trillion parameters, was put on three configurations with a 1,024-token input and a 400-token output. Eight AMD MI355X on SGLang, with ROCm fixes and speculative decoding from RadixArk's Kimi-K3-DSpark draft model, decoded at 118 tokens per second single-stream and peaked at 952 aggregate, 119 per GPU. Eight NVIDIA B300 beat that on every one of those three: 172 single-stream, 1,568 aggregate, 196 per GPU. A two-node, sixteen-GPU B200 configuration came last at 90, 498 and 31. On raw throughput the ordering is unambiguous and AMD loses — the B300 box returns about 1.65 times the aggregate tokens. The ordering inverts once the hour is priced: the B300 hour costs $6.00 against the MI355X's $2.50, 2.4 times as much for 1.65 times the tokens, so the AMD box comes out at about 48 tokens per second per dollar-hour against about 33 — roughly 1.45 times better on the axis that reaches an invoice, while losing on the axis a user feels. The two-node B200 configuration loses on both axes at once: about 7 tokens per second per dollar-hour on a $4.25 GPU-hour against the AMD box's 48, and 31 tokens per second per GPU, under a sixth of the eight-GPU B300 number. The author's explanation for that one is capacity rather than compute — enough HBM on the AMD box to hold a model this size without spanning nodes. But the comparison is not silicon against silicon, and today's bullet says as much in its own text: the speculative decoding credited with about 2.2 times the single-stream rate on the MI355X box has no counterpart described for either NVIDIA configuration, both of which the benchmark lists as running CUDA. Note what that does and does not establish — the bullet reports that no NVIDIA-side speculative-decoding setup is described, not that neither configuration used one, so this is an absence in the write-up rather than a demonstrated absence in the runs. Taken at face value, backing the 2.2 out of the MI355X's 118 leaves roughly 54, below even the two-node B200's 90. So software may be carrying a substantial share of a result that reads as a hardware verdict, and the cost inversion is better read as one described stack against another than as one vendor's parts against another's. One provenance note, because this item entered the corpus by weekend pickup rather than by publication: the benchmark was posted on Friday, July 31, two days before today and already published when yesterday's report was written, and it rests on a single source with no independent replication behind any of the figures — the same reservation yesterday's report attached to DeepSeek's vendor-reported benchmark table, now applied to hardware instead of a model.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events: two AI Tinkerers sessions fire and come off, Da Nang and a Palo Alto-hosted San Francisco summit are added, and Hot Chips swaps which half of its programme it reports
items.diff_narrative: The calendar moved in both directions and two listings left it, so it should not be read as carried forward. Two AI Tinkerers sessions have now fired and come off, and both departures are stated in the prose rather than left for a reader to notice by absence: the London session that yesterday's report listed for today, and the New York run-and-hack session that yesterday's report already recorded going on the day it fired. Two entries arrive. AI Tinkerers gains a newly-listed inaugural Da Nang meetup for Saturday, August 15, which extends the near-term run one date past the Bremen entry that ended it yesterday. And the Bay Area gains an event that collides with one already carried: the San Francisco AI Engineering and Infrastructure Summit on Thursday, October 15 — despite the name, at the Crowne Plaza Palo Alto on El Camino Real, 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM, free to attend, closed-door and practitioner-led with speakers already set rather than an open call — landing on the same Thursday as the separately-run AI Security Summit's San Francisco edition. That is now two Bay Area events on one date, and the new one is not in the city its name claims. Two entries changed state rather than detail. Black Hat USA 2026 was opening yesterday and is now underway, one day in at Mandalay Bay with trainings running through Tuesday, August 4, so the Las Vegas run is no longer prospective. The label moved with it, and this one is a correction rather than news: yesterday called the Black Hat-through-DEF CON span a security fortnight and today calls it a security stretch, which is the accurate word for August 1 to August 9 — nine days, not fourteen. IEEE-RAS Humanoids moves the same way: yesterday its workshop, tutorial and competition proposal deadline was the next open one on Monday, August 3; today it is tomorrow and identified as the last open submission window, so everything after it is a decision date rather than a submission date. Three listings traded detail, and one explains itself through its own source. Hot Chips swapped which half of its programme it reports: yesterday carried the full Sunday tutorial roster by name and cited the tutorial-day page, while today the tutorial day compresses to a memory session in the morning and a RISC-V session in the afternoon, the citation moves to the conference-day page, and the conference days come back thickened — the Waymo keynote on autonomous driving returns, and with it BOS Semiconductors' Eagle-N, AMD's secure computing system-on-chip alongside Versal RF in a Tuesday FPGA session, XCENA's MX1 CXL device and Mojo Vision's optical input-output, none of which appeared in yesterday's list. Its registration facts move both ways: today adds that late registration stays open through the conference itself subject to in-person capacity, and drops yesterday's note that nothing is refunded after August 19 and that credit cards are the only accepted payment. FMS runs the reverse trade, regaining its twentieth-year framing and losing Marvell's Mark Kuemerle and the 2:50 PM Wednesday keynote slot yesterday gave him. DEF CON's badge gains a third afterlife — a hardware security module on top of the security token and password manager. The AI Risk Summit regains the s'mores by the fire pits and adds post-conference materials, while shedding "Summer Summit" from the co-located CISO Forum's name and "Golf Links" from the golf venue; its price step is unchanged in substance, stated today as $1,895 stepping to $2,195 after Friday, August 7 rather than yesterday's $2,195 from Saturday, August 8. Zenity's call for papers tightens by one clause — submissions must now be practical rather than theoretical as well as vendor-agnostic — while the Asia edition stands exactly where yesterday left it: no city and no date on Zenity's own events page, and the third-party report giving it a Tokyo date in September still uncorroborated there and still explicitly not carried. The AI Security Summit's two San Francisco tracks are renamed rather than changed, leadership and practitioner where yesterday had the people who own risk and budgets and the people testing and breaking systems. The rest of the AI Tinkerers near-term list is the same dates with texture added rather than dates moved: Columbus gains a 5:30 to 8 PM EDT window, Paris a co-host in Paris.rb, Seattle's Tuesday an AI dev-tools track, Singapore a Redis partnership, the Seattle founders' dinner an Okta sponsorship, Medellín a $1,000 prize pool on an online voice-agents challenge, New York's Friday its Vision Hack name and 4 to 10 PM EDT hours, Mombasa an edge-AI and small-model framing for its chapter launch, Dubai a demo day, and the Seattle leg of the five-city Tuesday an AI-and-biology demo night with NVIDIA and the Allen Institute for AI. The Los Angeles meetup for Thursday, August 6 is still on the global listing and still carries the caveat that it briefly dropped off it at the end of last week. Ai4 and FMS each pick up a source of their own where yesterday they rode on the paragraph's general run. Everything else stands as carried: San Francisco, San Jose and Pleasanton remain undated, the Palo Alto and San Francisco chapter pages refused the connection again as they did yesterday so the Palo Alto meetup for Tuesday, August 18 is still unconfirmed at its own source, and the end-of-September San Francisco collision, the autumn sequence from World Summit AI through The AI Summit New York, the SANS, OWASP and ACM workshop dates in November, and Ray Summit's pricing and vLLM co-location are unchanged.
